title: Practice Period 5 - Sandokai
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up the closing lines of Shitou's Sandokai, recapping the poem in sets of eight lines before reading lines 33 to 42. The recap runs from the opening reassurance through the senses, the four elements, and the fish who cannot see water. Nomon notes that "principle" and "sameness" translate the same character, and the group wrestles with the image of two arrow points meeting midair. On "don't set up standards of your own," Nomon recalls a Zurich head student correcting the way a zafu was turned, and reads Suzuki Roshi on Tassajara's rules as the finger pointing at the moon. The session ends with the group's poems, including Nomon's about crows and a sidewalk.

sentences.text: **Nomon Tim Burnett:** *The mind of the great sage of India is intimately conveyed from west to east.
While you are sharp or dull, the ancestors, the spiritual source shines clear in the light, the branchy streams flow on in the dark.
Grasping at things is surely delusion, according to sameness is still not enlightenment.
All the objects of the senses interact and yet do not, interacting brings involvement, otherwise each keeps its place.
Sights vary in quality and form, sounds differ as pleasing or harsh, refined and common speech come together in the dark, clear and murky phrases are extinguished in the light.
The four elements return to their natures just as a child turns to its mother.
Fire heats, wind moves, water wets, earth is solid, eye and sights, hearing sounds, nose and mouth, tongue and taste.
Thus with each and everything depending on these roots the leaves spread forth, trunk and branches share the essence, revered in common each as its speech.
In the light there is darkness but don't take it as darkness, in the dark there is light but don't see it as light.
Light and dark oppose one another like the front and back foot in walking.
Each of the myriad things has its merit, expressed according to function in place.
Phenomena exist, box and lid fit, principle responds, arrow points meet.
Hearing the words understand the meaning, don't set up standards of your own.
If you don't understand the way right before you, how will you know the path as you walk?
Progress is not a matter of far or near, but if you are confused mountains and rivers block your way.
I respectfully urge you who study the mystery, do not pass your days and nights in vain.*
Well, it seems like reciting that together got a little more harmonious over five weeks, so may we accomplish that.
That's good.
Interesting, the way Suzuki Roshi talks about everything being all separate and independent, right?
Wasn't the whole gig all about interdependence?
So there are different ways to emphasize.
You can keep that in mind the next time your leg hurts and you're tempted to move it: it would be rude to disturb your leg's zazen.
Don't do that anymore.
Your leg needs some more space to practice.
This was in the context of monastic practice period, so they sit a lot there, as Kate can tell you, so maybe all their legs were hurting.
Apparently Suzuki Roshi's legs were hurting, or why would he have said that?
Anything strike you about that little passage from him?
What do you do when you get this really serious memo from your legs that says, I want to move now?
Yeah, well then the leg can move, it's independent, right?
A lot of this is about releasing ourselves from self-centeredness, that's a big theme.
Not to think "I'm sitting."
That was a big theme he always brought up, and I remember Blanche Hartman used to talk a lot about that.
She got all excited one time that she thought she was getting the hang of zazen, and so she went to see Suzuki Roshi and said, great news, I'm finally getting comfortable sitting zazen.
She thought he would just be like, oh, nice job, and instead he chewed her out.
He said, you don't do zazen, only zazen can do zazen, something like that.
At the time, I'm sure, really upsetting, but then thirty years later she thought it was a great story.
Who was that?
Suzuki Roshi and Blanche Hartman, who's on our table in there.
What were you going to say before, Linda?
**Participant:** One of my favorite things about Thich Nhat Hanh is that he says, all this pain, you don't have to do pain, don't do pain.
It probably depends on the context.
I also heard a talk with him, talking about how the important practice is to learn how to suffer well, to really do pain well.
**Nomon Tim Burnett:** In the context of sitting?
**Participant:** Yeah, well, I don't know, in the context of living.
**Nomon Tim Burnett:** Oh, well, this was about sitting.
About sitting, yeah, it doesn't need to hurt.
Yeah, well, there are pros and cons, right?
We don't want to hurt ourselves, or why would you keep coming?
On the other hand, aren't we retraining ourselves to a certain extent to not be so reactive about everything?
Can I just be with it and not react to it?
Because we're so reactive to everything, so maybe it's useful training, maybe there's usefulness to the commitment to sitting still, to just not need to react to things all the time.
But not to not react either, right?
That's also egotistical.
It's egotistical to think that you're sitting, it's egotistical to move, and it's egotistical to not move, so I don't know what you do.
So let's go back a little bit to the beginning of the text and I'll do a little recap.
This is like at the beginning of the TV show: last time on Sandokai.
I have this more or less divided into sets of eight lines.
It's not perfect, but it's a way to organize it.
So in the first set of eight, he named for us that there is really something here.
Something's being passed on to us.
Even though we may feel all kinds of ways about our abilities, whether we can understand or not understand, whether our faculties are sharp or dull, he says right away, no problem.
It doesn't matter where you're from, it doesn't matter if you're smart, you're not separate from this.
And we're all shining in the light and flowing in the darkness every moment, whether we know it or not.
So it starts out pretty affirming.
It's like, you're good, you're good.
But then he gives us a little warning, like lines seven and eight that we spent some time on.
Don't be so narrow-minded as to think that you can figure this out either.
So he opens with, it's okay, no problem, you've got this, and then he says, no, you can't get this.
You can't grasp the meaning of it.
And don't think that it's all about the opposite of that either.
Don't think it's just about releasing yourself from trying to get meaning and just resting in sameness or enlightenment or something like that.
That's not it either.
So the thrust of this teaching, and probably all teachings, and Dogen is especially explicit about this idea, is: study deeper, look more carefully, keep practicing.
There's always more to understand.
There's always further to go.
While at the same time there's nowhere to go.
He says that at the beginning, too.
And then lines nine to eighteen or so.
We get into how this actually plays out in daily life.
How does this unfold into the particulars of how we meet each moment?
And not to forget that even though we have all our high-falutin' ideas of what's going on, actually everything's just coming in through the senses.
And then we're doing stuff with all that sensory input, perceiving sounds as pleasant or harsh.
Then we're doing sense-making with that, processing it and expressing it.
Somebody brought up the way he talks about speech several times.
We're expressing, we're understanding, and you could be talking to yourself.
That's included.
This isn't just about making a speech to a group.
We're turning things into concepts and language, and that's part of what the speech piece is about.
So we can't help it.
And then it's a two-way street, with clear and murky and refined and common.
It's all in the dark and it's all in the light.
So the middle section of the poem is about, let's drop in on Jose and Jane and Javier, and I was trying to think of a Chinese name in there, Ying, and just see what's happening.
There's all this interaction and processing happening.
And then we get into the elements, lines 17 to 22, I guess.
Then don't get so worried about what you are, either, because you're just a bunch of elements, actually.
You're the five skandhas, you're the four elements coming together in this moment in this configuration that seems to be self-aware and everything.
But really you're just fire, like heat.
You feel your heat, your wind, your water, your earth.
Buddhism actually usually emphasizes a fifth element, the element of space, that he doesn't mention.
I don't know why, but he doesn't.
And space, of course, is the most important element, because everything is full of space.
The ancients figured this out way before nuclear physics.
I forget what percentage of an atom is actually stuff, but it's really, really tiny.
Minuscule.
And yet it all seems so solid.
So we're mostly made out of space with a little dash of fire, wind, water, and earth just tossed in there.
Mostly space.
And all that stuff comes together and interacts in all kinds of weird ways.
And then when we get to line 25 or so, just to recognize that all these conditions lead to some expression.
So it's not like there isn't something here.
Something's being expressed: according to these roots the leaves spread forth.
Something called a life or a universe is being expressed.
But it's not exactly itself either.
It's an expression of all these other things too.
And then in about line 27, we're back to dark and light.
Back to this theme that waves through all of Mahayana Buddhism: form and emptiness, dark and light, ji and ri.
When I was looking at this again, I was thinking about the famous metaphor, so ancient, of a fish swimming in the water or a bird flying in the air, which Dogen makes heavy use of too.
It's such a good metaphor.
This idea that we can see the fishes in the water.
Hi, fish.
You're swimming in water, and the fish is like, what are you talking about?
This is just my life.
There's no such thing.
What's water?
So what's air if you're a bird?
So what this is trying to describe, Zen awakening, whatever you want to call it, we can't really call it anything, just like the fish doesn't have a word for water.
We don't have a word for what this is exactly.
Well, we have lots of words to try to triangulate it.
And maybe that would be how you'd try to explain water to the fish.
We have this feeling of flowing, this kind of fluid feeling.
You know that feeling, and the fish is like, yeah, yeah, that's water.
What?
So it's like that.
For us, emptiness, we're like, what?
And the Buddha is like, no, no, you're in it.
It's just you.
What?
So Master Shitou is trying to help us understand this in a million different ways.
So that brings us to the last dozen lines, starting at line 33.
Are you ready?
Hold on to your hats.
I'll just read that out loud.
You can read with your eyes or listen.
So how is he ending?
We know the setup, so how is this going to end?
What's the exciting conclusion of Sandokai?
*Each of the myriad things has its merit, expressed according to function and place.
Phenomena exist, box and lid fit, principle responds, arrow points meet.
Hearing the words, understand the meaning.
Don't set up standards of your own.
If you don't understand the way right before you, how will you know the path as you walk?
Progress is not a matter of far or near.
But if you are confused, mountains and rivers block your way.
Respectfully urge you to study the mystery.
Do not pass your days and nights in vain.*
So lines 35 and 36, we're back for the second time to the actual characters, G and V.
Are you excited?
The first character of line 35 is G: phenomena, things, stuff.
It's on the Han too.
So there's G: phenomena exist, box and lid fit.
And the first character of line 36, which here is translated as principle, and maybe you remember way back to line 8, there they used a different English word, it's translated as sameness.
So we're using different English words for the same character.
It's interesting, huh?
But it's the same idea.
Except here, instead of just talking about the reality of this, we're appreciating it.
There's a real sense of appreciation here, isn't there?
Phenomena, the G, the stuff in the light, the stuff we can see and name and conceptualize, it's like a box and a lid.
It just fits together.
Astounding.
We're so used to that we don't notice.
This is a little more like the water and the fish.
The door sits in its hinges and closes, and the lectern sits on the floor.
And it's not just physical stuff, remember.
It's also our thoughts and our bodies and all the things that we can perceive and talk about.
Somehow it's all fitting together, amazing.
Of course our mind gets focused on the things that we don't think fit together, but this is the essential quality of this: it all somehow fits together.

But then line 36 is like, well, even the things in the dark, even this principle, this unknowability, even this emptiness, even though you can't see it or talk about it exactly, somehow it responds and it just meets what it needs to meet, like two arrow points.
That's a famous story about archers: even the best archer can hit the target, but how did two arrows hit?
And the other thing that's kind of fun is that this poem and the other Chinese poem in our chant book use some of the same images.
The image of the arrow points meeting is in both poems.
So it's an old Chinese story.

So we're ending here, after all this exploration, with a sense of appreciation, like wow, everything in the world of ji and everything in the world of ri just responds and fits, and there's this weird organic functioning, it's all happening.
Go ahead, Chris.
**Participant:** Arrow points meeting midair is like Mission Impossible.
So it's like so self-evident, he says phenomena exist, box and lids fit.
I know plenty of lids that don't fit, but that's not the point.
The principle responds, arrow points meet, they don't.
I mean, it's an incredible coincidence if they actually do meet, you can't make it happen.
So I'm just wondering how that fits into this narrative.
**Nomon Tim Burnett:** What does everyone think?
**Participant:** There was a story in here that did happen.
I've forgotten.
**Nomon Tim Burnett:** Well, it's the same as the Chinese story where it happened.
But it's just a story, right?
It talks about how extraordinary it is, actually.
Those arrow points do meet midair.
Well, there's a lot of ways we could look at it.
What does everyone else think about this idea?
**Participant:** My first thought, before I had the story, was that I remember the Battle of Hastings and many other battles where the ultimate weapon was the group of archers.
If your mass of archers is doing their thing before the battle, as is the other group of archers, they knock each other out of the air all the time.
But that's how I took it before I read this.
Literally like battle and archers.
But yeah, the deeper story here may be about the idea of possibility and impossibility.
Box and lid seems very possible and arrow points meeting seems impossible, right?
It's also one you understand in your day to day life.
It's the G, and the other one you don't understand and it never happens unless the Rui.
He's deliberately bringing up an impossible situation to say, yeah, of course, impossible.
He says it like it happens all the time.
**Participant:** Yeah, I read it a little bit like what Ken was saying, that he's deliberately bringing up the impossible in this very everyday way to remind us not to feel so limited.
So that's like the form of emptiness, right?
Not to feel so limited by our ideas of what's possible.
I think we actually do have experiences too that seem impossible, like whoa, how did that happen?
Could it be something like life makes sense even though you may not think that way?
Or you may think that's impossible?
It makes sense in a way you can't possibly imagine?
**Nomon Tim Burnett:** Yeah.
Other thoughts about impossibility?
**Participant:** I looked at it as going back to the common and refined, such exposition of these two extremes that are just part of life.
**Nomon Tim Burnett:** Yeah, I mean, when you think about it, possible and impossible are extreme ideas.
It's the real nature of reality, dividable in that way.
Thank you.
Yeah, thank you.
That's a good question.
All right, let's plunge into the next set of lines.
So lines 35 and 36, I think, are a little moment of just enthusiasm.
Master Shirito is like, yes!
And now he's going to give us advice.
We're leaving with practice advice.
So: *hearing the words, understand the meeting.
Don't set up standards of your own.
If you're to understand the way right before you, how will you know the ways you walk?
Progress is not a matter of far or near, but if you are confused, mountains and rivers block your way.
Respectfully urge you who study the mystery.
Do not pass your days and nights in vain.* So let's take that one line at a time, and I'll give you my thoughts and you can pause and see what you think.
So, hearing the words, understand the meaning.
One thing I think about that is that the singular "the" is maybe a little problematic, and the Chinese doesn't have that article, actually.
They don't have singular and plural articles.
So is there really the meaning or a meaning?
Let's dip into the source on this one.
This one is actually kind of fun.
It's the second verse on the second-to-last page of the bigger handout.
Where we have "hearing the words, understand the meaning," the literal characters mean something more like "receive doctrine."
So: receive words, must understand, and then there's the word for lineage.
That gets left out of English.
So maybe this is not as global as it sounds.
Maybe it's: hear these teachings and understand them according to the lineage of Master Shitou.
That's interesting, because how could there be one meaning?
Just one meaning doesn't seem to fit the rest of the text.
Hear the words in light of a particular way of doing meaning.
What did you think about "hearing the words, understand the meaning"?
Is that just a simple idea, where we can get it right or get it wrong?
But doesn't every word have multiple meanings?
Even if you have a group of people using the same words, you just assume everyone understands them the same way, but you're wrong.
Everyone's understanding things a little bit differently.
Any thoughts about that line?
It's setting us up for the next line: words as doctrine, which is like teaching.
So, receive the teaching according to the lineage from the Buddha, which is a little different.
Does lineage here literally mean the line of ancestors?
Yeah, like ancestral lineage.
Pretty sure.
You've got the Chinese there, you can go look it up.
So now we have "don't set up standards of your own."
This is a very interesting line.
It's probably my favorite line of this whole text, and it's like a koan for us whenever we're making decisions around here.
It's our constant koan.
It has come up in many a meeting and many a calm or heated moment in the zendo: do we do it this way or do we do it that way?
Don't make standards of your own.
And yet we have to adapt and change at the same time.
So we receive something, this tradition, and here we are trying to do it in American culture, in Bellingham, in the twenty-first century.
We've got to make some changes, probably, for it to make any kind of sense.
And yet it seems so narrow-minded to just change it to suit our preferences.
A little bit like what Suzuki Roshi was saying during the zazen thing: don't be egotistical and just make it suit your wishes and your whims.
So maybe there's something in this format of practice we've received that is useful even though we don't like it.
Or maybe we haven't understood it yet, or it hasn't landed yet.
Maybe these things take a hundred years.
What do we know?

On the other hand, an evolution that's been interesting for me: when I was first practicing at the Zen centers that Suzuki Roshi founded, there was this idea in the air that there was a particular way they do it in Japan, and we had to do it that way.
Oftentimes that would be the way these arguments would end there, back then.
This was in the late eighties; it's probably different now.
They'd say, "Oh no, this is the way they do it in Japan.
That's the final word."
Then eventually I went to Japan.
We went to different temples, and they did it different ways.
One place they offer the incense this way, one place they do it that way.
So there's not actually any one way they do it in Japan.
So are they making up standards of their own?
Is it a communal thing?
Does it just need to happen slowly?
And then how about in our lives?
This is just the example of the Zen form, which is one particular example.
We treasure individuality.
We treasure finding our own way.
And yet aren't we also trying, in some way, to honor what we received?
And how do we do that in a way that's authentic?
On this issue of the Zen form as an example of all this, Suzuki Roshi had some nice comments in the book.
I'll share a few with you.
One of the things he said was:
*Rules are very important in our practice.
We are liable to establish our own rules.
This is the rule of Tassajara, you might say.
The rules are the finger that points to how we have good practice at Tassajara according to the situation.
Rules are important, but you shouldn't think this is the only way.
Our rules are true teachings, or their rules are wrong.
You shouldn't stick to your own understanding of things.
What is good for one person isn't always good for another.
So you should not make rules for everyone.
Rules are important.
But don't stick to rules and don't force them on others.*
Then about half a page later he says:
*When you enter monastery you shouldn't say, I have my own way.
If you come to Tassajara you should follow Tassajara's rules.
Don't establish your own rules.*
So he said it both ways.
But this is beautiful here:
*To see the actual moon through Tassajara rules is the way to practice at Tassajara.
Rules are not the point.
The teaching that the rules will catch is the point.
By observing the rules you will naturally understand the real teaching.*
Earlier he said the finger, so here he's playing off the finger and the moon.
*To see the actual moon through Tassajara is the way to practice at Tassajara.
Rules are not the point.
The teaching that the rules will catch is the point.
The teaching that the rules will catch is the point.
By observing the rules you will naturally understand the real teaching.*
I'm sure all of us have lots of examples of encountering rules in different ways, of setting up standards of your own, and there's a certain tension you feel: am I just trying to do it my way?
What's great about Zen is we get really picky in a way that brings it up in your face, in a way that you can see it and wonder about it.
I was remembering an example in my life.
One time I went and sat for the morning at the Zen Center in Zurich in Switzerland.
All the explanation and the Dharma talk were in German, so I was a little bit at sea.
Of course, it turned out they all spoke English once they figured out who I was.
But anyway, after zazen, with the talk during zazen, we were out in the lobby, and the head student comes trundling up to me and starts talking to me in high-speed German.
I say, "I'm sorry, I don't speak German."
He switches to English and says, "You had your zafu backwards."
I said, "Huh?"
These ones don't have it, but the zafus on this little kind of handily placed had this white tag.
I think I do this when I'm thinking about it.
I just said, "Oh look at that, kind of bright white tag."
So I turned it so it was facing the wall, so no one would be bothered by my white tag.
But it turns out their form was the tag face in, and they should be lined up exactly this way.
And so this guy who had been practicing there forever looked around the room, as you do, and, huh?
I admit that I felt a little defensive.
I thought, this is the way you're going to greet a brand new guest at your zazen center?
Really?
My zafu was backwards?
I got a little defensive, you know?
Seriously?
But then we went up and had coffee, a really strong coffee.
They all realized who I was and were super friendly and nice.
They all switched to English so I'd understand, and I had the loveliest time.
So, was the head student chewing me out and messing with me?
Was I setting up standards of my own, or was it just information?
And we do this with everything, right?
With everything.
So it's an interesting teaching in this poem: don't set up standards of your own.
This is a deep thing to consider.
What comes up for you around that?
**Participant:** I think there's a huge cultural thing: Western European and especially American culture is so much about the individual, and Eastern societies are so much about the collective.
And it's just fundamentally this.
I think this whole discussion would be different if it wasn't the thing.
So I'm sure it's not a thing.
I think for your own it would be much less difficult to swallow.
Yeah.
Maybe it's more important for us then.
They already have that, you know.
I think it's maybe when the ego speaks up and, "Oh, I wanted this way, I wanted just like so," and the group consensus is different.
If I focus on my wishes, my desire, it's like this big issue.
I get upset over it and think about ways around it.
But if I can just drop it, then there's no problem.
**Nomon Tim Burnett:** Yeah.
So, does individualism equal suffering?
Huh?
That's an interesting question.
**Participant:** Maybe not always, but yeah, pretty often, I think.
It really doesn't matter which way the zafus turn, you know?
It doesn't matter, but the zendo has it this way.
**Nomon Tim Burnett:** Yeah.

That's wrong.

**Nomon Tim Burnett:** We can stick with the [unclear: "uploaders"], as long as we agree.

**Participant:** For some reason I'm flashing up: a student taught up at Western for English as a second language, and they were teaching grammar, and I could just remember saying, "You've got to know the rules before you can break them," and this whole group of Japanese boys in the back just really good.

*If you don't understand the way right before you, how will you know the path as you walk?
Progress is not a matter of far or near, but if you are confused, mountains and rivers block your way.*
That's interesting.
Is there progress?
Is there a path we're walking?
And this text really seems to be saying yes and no, right?
On the one hand, you need to know the way right before you.
On the other hand, if you're too sure you know the way right before you, you're wrong, right?
That's confused.
That's mountains and rivers blocking your way.
I think we all have that experience about this.
Whenever you're too sure, there's trouble.
But if you are completely at sea, that's another kind of trouble.
So there's something here about progress, about practice.
What does this practice result in?
How do we know which direction to go?
There is a direction and there's no direction.
So this is just an open-ended thing, this question of progress.
On the one hand, we know that if we try to [unclear: "mix us"] and do something, we'll pretty much suffer, right?
On the other hand, if there's no progress, if there's no benefit, if there's no way to walk, why are you wasting your time here anyway?
So this is interesting to hold: how do I see my progress?
How do I see my path?
Do I think I know where that is?
Do I think there is one or isn't one?
And when do I feel stuck?
I like this last line about mountains and rivers blocking your way.
I thought about this a little more, and I thought, no, it's not mountains and rivers that block my way.
It's me.
I walk my way, right?
